records.name: Breast conservation or mastectomy
records.tldr: For eligible early breast cancers, trials found no significant survival difference between breast conservation with radiation and mastectomy. Local recurrence and the rest of the treatment plan still matter.
records.summary:
Four randomised trials settled this and all four reported at twenty years or more. NSABP B-06 randomised 1,851 women three ways and found no significant difference in disease-free, distant-disease-free or overall survival between total mastectomy, lumpectomy alone and lumpectomy with irradiation; the hazard ratio for death after lumpectomy with irradiation against mastectomy was 0.97 (95 percent confidence interval 0.83 to 1.14). Milan I randomised 701 women to Halsted radical mastectomy or quadrantectomy with radiotherapy and found death from any cause at twenty years of 41.2 and 41.7 percent (p=1.0). EORTC 10801 randomised 868 patients including tumours up to 5 cm and found time to death at a median 22.1 years no different (hazard ratio 1.11, 0.94 to 1.33). NSABP B-04, at twenty-five years, found no advantage to radical mastectomy over lesser operations at all.

What does differ is the chance of the cancer returning in the breast that was kept: 14.3 percent at twenty years in NSABP B-06 with radiotherapy, against 39.2 percent without it, and 8.8 against 2.3 percent between quadrantectomy and radical mastectomy in Milan I. A recurrence in a conserved breast is usually salvageable by mastectomy, which is part of why survival is unaffected: in the EORTC boost trial, mastectomy was the first salvage treatment for 279 of 354 such recurrences (79 percent) in one arm and 178 of 237 (75 percent) in the other.

Mastectomy is still the right operation for some: a tumour too large for the breast to give a good result, several tumours in different quadrants, inflammatory breast cancer, a margin that cannot be cleared by re-excision, a woman who cannot have radiotherapy, and a woman who has weighed the options and wants the breast off. Risk-reducing mastectomy in a BRCA1 or BRCA2 carrier is a different operation for a different reason.

In England NICE NG101 recommendation 1.4.3 offers further surgery when tumour is at the inked margin, and recommendation 1.4.5 considers it when tumour cells lie within 1 mm of the radial margin, a threshold the guideline lowered from 2 mm in 2024 to reduce re-operations.

notes: Lumpectomy, partial mastectomy and segmental excision can describe breast-conserving removal of a lesion with surrounding tissue. Mastectomy removes breast tissue more extensively. Skin-sparing and nipple-sparing variants retain selected outer structures while removing the underlying gland; retained skin does not mean the gland remains.

The breast operation does not specify the nodal procedure, final margins or reconstruction. Mastectomy with sentinel biopsy does not mean axillary dissection. Reconstruction reshapes or restores the breast area and does not replace cancer treatment. Either breast operation can be accompanied by radiation or systemic medicines as the setting requires.

At 20 years, Fisher and colleagues' NSABP B-06 report included 1851 women with follow-up and known nodal status and found no significant overall-survival difference among total mastectomy, lumpectomy and lumpectomy with irradiation. The death hazard ratio for lumpectomy with irradiation versus mastectomy was 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.14). Ipsilateral recurrence was 14.3% with breast irradiation versus 39.2% without; survival and local recurrence are different endpoints.

Veronesi and colleagues' Milan I trial enrolled 701 women with tumours no larger than 2 cm. At median 20 years, all-cause death was 41.2% after radical mastectomy and 41.7% after quadrantectomy with radiation. These eligible historical trial populations do not establish exact equality for every contemporary person or every disease setting.

Compare complete plans and eligibility, including lesion distribution and size relative to breast, margin findings, radiation feasibility, prior treatment, inherited risk and preferences. A larger operation does not automatically establish a survival gain. Negative margins describe evaluated local boundaries, not whole-body absence of cancer.

The amount removed and resulting breast shape vary with the lesion and operation. An illustrative breast-excision sketch does not promise an unchanged shape or show a nodal operation. Retaining skin or nipple structures differs from retaining the underlying gland; read the operative report and nodal procedure separately.

In Milan I, local recurrence at 20 years was 8.8% after quadrantectomy with radiation versus 2.3% after radical mastectomy, despite no significant survival difference. B-06 separately compared lumpectomy with and without radiation. These comparisons do not establish equal local recurrence or quantify that radiation closes most of a mastectomy-versus-conservation gap.

records.name: Breast reconstruction
records.tldr: Rebuilding the shape of a breast after a mastectomy, either with an implant or with the woman's own tissue, at the same operation or years later. In England every woman having a mastectomy for breast cancer must be offered it, and must be offered both timings whether or not the local hospital provides them.
records.summary:
There are two families of technique. Implant-based reconstruction uses a silicone implant, either placed at the mastectomy (direct to implant) or after a tissue expander has stretched the skin, and either behind the pectoralis major (sub-pectoral) or in front of it (pre-pectoral). Autologous reconstruction moves the woman's own skin and fat, most often from the lower abdomen as a deep inferior epigastric perforator flap, which spares the rectus muscle, and less often from the back (latissimus dorsi) or elsewhere. Reconstruction is immediate, at the same operation as the mastectomy, or delayed.

The honest comparison comes from the Mastectomy Reconstruction Outcomes Consortium, which followed 2,343 women for two years with both complications and a validated patient-reported questionnaire. Autologous reconstruction gave better satisfaction with the breasts (7.94 points higher, 5.68 to 10.20, p<0.001), psychosocial wellbeing and sexual wellbeing at two years. It also roughly doubled the odds of a complication: 1.97 (1.41 to 2.76) for a deep inferior epigastric perforator flap against expander-implant reconstruction. Implants failed more often, 7.1 percent against 1.3 percent for those flaps.

British practice has been measured twice and neither reading is comfortable. In iBRA, 2,081 women having immediate implant-based reconstruction at 81 units had implant loss of 9 percent, infection needing treatment of 25 percent, return to theatre of 18 percent and readmission of 18 percent within three months, all above the National Quality Standards of under 5 percent for the first three and under 10 percent for infection. Pre-BRA followed the newer pre-pectoral technique in 343 women and found implant loss of 8.2 percent and a complication in 42.0 percent, with physical and sexual wellbeing significantly below baseline at three and eighteen months.

The mesh question is unresolved. Biological or synthetic mesh, including acellular dermal matrix, is used to support the implant, and in iBRA 65 percent of reconstructions used it, 54 percent biological and 12 percent synthetic, without randomised evidence that it helps. Best-BRA, a pilot randomised trial of pre-pectoral against sub-pectoral placement, is the attempt to put that right.

On timing, NICE NG101 recommendation 1.5.1 offers reconstruction to everyone after a mastectomy for breast cancer, 1.5.3 offers both immediate and delayed options whether or not they are available locally, and 1.5.4 offers immediate reconstruction even to women who may need radiotherapy, unless another illness rules out the surgery. The guideline's own table warns that immediate reconstruction using implants may be affected by radiotherapy more than immediate flap reconstruction, and recommendation 1.13.14 allows the three-week radiotherapy schedule rather than the one-week one for women who have had implant-based reconstruction.

Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a rare cancer of the capsule around an implant and is covered separately.

records.name: Sentinel lymph node biopsy
records.tldr: Sentinel lymph node biopsy identifies and samples the first draining node or nodes to assess spread. The sampled result does not describe every node or prove whole-body absence.
records.summary:
A tracer and mapping method identify one or more first-draining lymph nodes, which are removed for pathological examination. The procedure and sampled tissue result are different records. Technique, pretreatment findings and treatment timing affect interpretation; sentinel-node biopsy is not a guarantee that every involved node was found.

Z0011 and AMAROS tested specified surgery-first treatment strategies after positive sentinel findings. Their populations and accompanying radiation matter. Residual positive sentinel nodes after neoadjuvant treatment are a different question, studied by A011202. Avoid turning these comparisons into a universal rule that every positive node needs dissection or that no further axillary treatment is ever needed.

records.name: Thermal ablation (RFA, microwave, cryo)
records.tldr: Thermal ablation uses an applicator to heat or freeze selected tissue. Safe coverage and later local control need assessment beyond placing the device.
records.summary:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

notes: BOOSTER studied ablation added to continuing immunotherapy in selected advanced lung cancer with limited residual disease after response. It was not an SBRT trial or a comparison in every metastatic setting. Cryo-versus-heating comparisons within that small trial were exploratory rather than a randomised test of the two modalities.

Record the method, applicator settings such as power in watts, exposure time, measured temperature in degrees Celsius where relevant, and three-dimensional zone or margin measurements with the imaging method and assessment time. A generator setting or one sensor does not measure exposure everywhere or count viable cells.

BOOSTER randomised 65 selected patients with residual advanced lung cancer after checkpoint treatment, rather than the planned 137; its primary analysis included 42 with ablation and twenty without. The primary progression-free-survival clock began at immunotherapy initiation, before randomisation, so its medians of 26.7 versus 11.7 months include a selected pre-entry period. The report separately gives a randomisation-clock analysis of 17.1 versus 4.4 months. These clocks cannot be exchanged when comparing headlines. The physician selected freezing or heating: the abstract says thirteen cryoablation and 31 thermal-ablation patients, whereas Figure 3 and the discussion say thirteen and 29 among the 42 analysed. The discussion also notes larger lesions in the thermal group and no correction for multiple comparisons. This internally discrepant, exploratory comparison does not establish universal superiority of freezing or an immune-optimal modality.

Colorectal metastases: NICE NG151 says to consider chemotherapy with local ablative techniques for colorectal liver metastases unsuitable for liver resection, and to consider metastasectomy, ablation or stereotactic body radiation therapy for lung metastases suitable for local treatment after discussion by a multidisciplinary team that includes a thoracic surgeon and a specialist in non-surgical ablation.
records.principle: An applicator transfers heat into tissue or extracts it. The spatial and temporal exposure, tissue properties and blood flow influence the resulting injury.
strengths: Can treat a selected site without removing the whole organ
Image guidance supports access and assessment of the treatment zone
limitations: Access, geometry and nearby normal structures can limit coverage
Blood flow and device/tissue properties affect exposure
Imaging and later assessment are needed; visible coverage alone is insufficient

records.name: SBRT / SABR (stereotactic radiotherapy)
records.tldr: Stereotactic body radiotherapy delivers a high dose per treatment to a defined body target using specialised localisation and verification. A short schedule alone does not identify it or establish safety.
records.summary:
Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

records.name: Surgical resection specimen
records.tldr: Removed tissue becomes interpretable through documented orientation and sampling that link microscopic and molecular findings to their locations.
records.summary: A resection specimen is removed tissue submitted for examination. The laboratory documents gross features, marks relevant surfaces and maps selected regions into labelled blocks. Microscopy and additional assays describe the represented material, rather than every cell remaining in the body.

links.label: CAP practical breast grossing guide excerpt

notes: Keep the specimen site, procedure, prior treatment, orientation key, surface inks, cassette map and tested block with the result. Ink colours have a local documented meaning. Gross specimen dimensions are not automatically invasive tumour dimensions. Fragmentation or ink entering cracks can complicate surface interpretation.

Fictional example: block A is central lesion and block B is a superior surface. A sequencing result from block A cannot be assigned to block B merely because both came from one operation. An additional test needs its own block identity and preservation history.

Resection supports assessment of represented tumour extent, surfaces, sampled nodes and treatment effect. A large specimen is not automatically examined cell by cell in its entirety. Collection time and preceding treatment define the biological time point, so a post-treatment resection cannot substitute for a pretreatment biopsy.

Diagnostic orientation and mapped sampling must remain intact when additional material is allocated. A research aliquot needs its site, block, preservation, treatment context and permissions. Slide counts alone do not establish the completeness of representation; a clear examined margin does not settle every clinical question.

Resection examination follows receipt and orientation, gross description, block mapping, microscopic examination and integration of findings. Record the named specimen and separately submitted parts; sectioning and extraction consume finite material. Depending on the cancer, specimen and treatment setting, outputs include diagnoses, dimensions and distances in millimetres, described margins and sampled-node counts. Lost orientation, fragmentation, ink penetration, incomplete mapping and unsuitable preservation can limit interpretation. Applicable diagnostic protocols and clinical correlation govern the report, while a research aliquot needs its own provenance. No specimen report examines every tissue left in the body or every unsampled node, or supplies an individual recurrence probability.

records.name: Radiotherapy
records.tldr: Radiotherapy deposits ionising radiation in tissue to damage cancer cells. The target, normal tissues, treatment schedule and clinical goal all matter.
records.summary:
Radiation transfers energy to tissue and can damage DNA directly or through reactive molecules. Cells can repair damage or lose their ability to keep dividing, and death can occur later. One treatment session is an exposure, rather than an immediate count of dead cells. Oxygen, cell state and repair affect the response.

External beams, brachytherapy sources and systemically distributed radiopharmaceuticals have different exposure patterns. An external-beam target can include tissue at risk of microscopic disease after surgery, even when no mass is visible. Planning and verification consider geometry, motion, normal organs and previous overlapping exposure. Precision does not eliminate normal-tissue dose or injury.

Absorbed dose in gray is energy per mass: one gray is one joule per kilogram. Total dose, fraction size, timing and exposed volume influence biological effects. Physical-dose arithmetic alone does not establish equivalence of schedules. Local or regional control, symptom relief, distant disease and survival remain distinct clinical outcomes.

records.name: Mastectomy
records.tldr: Mastectomy removes breast tissue. The exact operation, nodal procedure and reconstruction are separate parts of the plan, and removal does not automatically eliminate the need for radiation or medicines.
records.summary:
Different mastectomy procedures remove different skin, nipple or chest-wall structures and may be accompanied by a separate nodal operation. The operative report specifies what was removed; pathology describes the examined tissue and boundaries. Neither the operation’s name nor a negative local finding establishes the absence of cancer throughout the body.

Reconstruction can use implants or a person’s tissue and may occur immediately or later. It addresses restoration or reshaping, rather than replacing indicated cancer treatment. Radiation and systemic therapy decisions retain disease extent, prior treatment and the full plan; a margin finding does not universally choose completion mastectomy over another approach.

notes: Read the breast-conserving surgery versus mastectomy comparison for differences in gland removal, retained skin or nipple, local recurrence and survival evidence. The breast operation does not specify the nodal operation, final margins or reconstruction; record each separately.

Triple-negative breast cancer, reconstruction timing: NICE NG101 says offer reconstruction after mastectomy, offer both immediate and delayed options whether or not they are available locally, and offer immediate reconstruction to women advised to have a mastectomy including those who may need radiotherapy; its table notes that implant reconstructions may be more affected by radiotherapy than flap reconstructions and that complications can delay chemotherapy or radiotherapy. The NHS says recovery takes several weeks, with wounds healing in about 6 weeks. Macmillan says you may choose no reconstruction and wear a prosthesis instead.

When a mastectomy is recommended rather than chosen. Macmillan says surgeons try to do an operation that means you can keep your breast, and that a mastectomy may be recommended when the lump is large compared to the rest of the breast, when there is cancer in different parts of the breast (multicentric), when there is widespread DCIS, when the cancer is on the skin or in the underlying muscle, when you have had radiotherapy to the chest before to treat another cancer, or when you have a family history and have tested positive for a gene mutation.

A mastectomy does not always avoid radiotherapy. NICE NG101 (1.13.10) says to offer adjuvant postmastectomy radiotherapy to people with node-positive (macrometastases) invasive breast cancer or involved resection margins, (1.13.11) to consider it for node-negative T3 or T4 disease, and (1.13.12) not to offer it to people at low risk of local recurrence, for example most people with lymph node-negative breast cancer.

NICE NG101 (1.5.1) says to offer breast reconstruction to people after they have had a mastectomy for breast cancer, and (1.5.2) to be aware that some people may prefer not to have it. Cancer Research UK says a surgeon may be able to improve the appearance of the chest with further surgery after a mastectomy, and that a prosthesis is an alternative to reconstruction.

records.name: Lumpectomy (breast-conserving surgery)
records.tldr: Lumpectomy removes a breast tumour with surrounding tissue while preserving the rest of the breast. Margin findings, nodal procedures and other treatments need separate description.
records.summary:
The removed tissue is examined by pathology, including its cut boundaries and any separately submitted margins. The operation’s name does not establish a negative final margin, specify the nodal procedure or exclude microscopic disease elsewhere. A further operation depends on the findings and applicable clinical standard, rather than the word lumpectomy alone.

Breast-conserving treatment commonly includes radiation, and medicines may be given before or after surgery. Oncoplastic reshaping or later reconstruction is a separate role. Compare complete treatment plans, local outcomes, recovery and harms; greater removal does not automatically establish better survival for every person.

notes: Read the breast-conserving surgery versus mastectomy comparison for differences in gland removal, retained skin or nipple, local recurrence and survival evidence. The breast operation does not specify the nodal operation, final margins or reconstruction; record each separately.

In triple-negative breast cancer chemotherapy is usually given first, and Cancer Research UK says shrinking the cancer may allow breast-conserving surgery instead of a mastectomy. Macmillan says breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy is usually as effective as a mastectomy and that a second operation is needed if cancer is at the margin; NICE NG101 (2024) asks for further surgery when invasive cancer is at the radial margin and to consider it within 1 mm.

Breast cancer, the long-term comparison with mastectomy. In the Milan trial, 701 women with breast cancers no larger than 2 cm were randomly assigned between 1973 and 1980 to radical (Halsted) mastectomy (349) or quadrantectomy followed by radiotherapy (352). After a median 20 years of follow-up, death from any cause had occurred in 41.2 percent of the radical mastectomy group and 41.7 percent of the conserving surgery group (P equals 1.0), and death from breast cancer in 24.3 and 26.1 percent (P equals 0.8). What differed was the breast: 30 women in the conserving group had a recurrence in the same breast against 8 local recurrences after radical mastectomy, a crude cumulative incidence of 8.8 against 2.3 percent, with no significant difference in contralateral cancers, distant metastases or second primary cancers.

In NSABP B-06, 1,851 women were randomly assigned to total mastectomy, lumpectomy alone, or lumpectomy with breast irradiation, and followed for 20 years. Recurrence in the same breast occurred in 14.3 percent of those given radiotherapy against 39.2 percent of those not (P less than 0.001), and no significant difference was found between the three groups in disease-free survival, distant-disease-free survival or overall survival: the hazard ratio for death was 1.05 (0.90 to 1.23) for lumpectomy alone against total mastectomy and 0.97 (0.83 to 1.14) for lumpectomy with irradiation.

NICE NG101 (1.13.3) says to offer whole-breast radiotherapy to women with invasive breast cancer who have had breast-conserving surgery with clear margins, and (1.13.4, 1.13.5) to consider partial-breast radiotherapy for women aged 50 and over with tumours 3 cm or less that are N0, ER-positive, HER2-negative and grade 1 to 2 who will take endocrine therapy for at least 5 years, telling them that local recurrence at 5 years is equivalent, that the risk beyond 5 years is not yet known, and that late adverse effects may be reduced.

records.name: Sentinel node biopsy
records.tldr: Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and examines selected draining nodes. Its result describes that sampling procedure, with limits that depend on the disease and treatment setting.
records.summary:
A dye, radiotracer or other mapping agent identifies draining nodes for removal and pathological examination. Sentinel sampling and broader nodal dissection provide different amounts of tissue and have different risks. Neither a negative sampled node nor the operation name establishes the status of every regional node or distant organ.

The NCI fact sheet describes a radioactive tracer, blue dye or both for mapping. It identifies breast cancer and melanoma as the most common uses and notes use or investigation in other cancers, including endometrial, penile, vulvar, cervical and head-and-neck disease. Eligibility and the next operation depend on the disease-specific setting; a negative result can be false negative. A thickness threshold used in melanoma must not be transferred to breast cancer.

notes: Sentinel biopsy removes tracer-identified draining nodes for pathological examination; there can be more than one. Axillary dissection removes a broader tissue packet from specified axillary levels, not every regional chain and not a universally fixed number of nodes. CAP separately uses the sn modifier when fewer than six sentinel and nonsentinel nodes are removed.

For retrieval of a previously marked positive node after neoadjuvant therapy and the Z1071 and clipped-node false-negative analyses, see targeted axillary dissection. Sentinel mapping alone does not document recovery of that separate marker.

False-negative rate compares the sampled test with a defined reference among those with disease. Nodal surgery can cause lymphoedema and other harms; sentinel biopsy is not risk-free and dissection does not guarantee complications. A positive sentinel result does not select one universal subsequent operation without the full treatment setting.

In a fictional mapping sketch, tracer-identified nodes A and B and a separately clipped node C may overlap: one node can carry both designations. A wider packet outline depicts broader sampling. Mapping lines are procedural tracing, not observed routes of cancer spread. A negative sentinel result cannot establish that C was retrieved.

Isolated tumour cells and micrometastases are reported differently under nodal classification; a binary positive/negative label can hide those distinctions. A false-negative rate needs the tested procedure, reference assessment and denominator with disease. It is not the probability that every negative result missed disease, and it says nothing about all distant organs.

Breast cancer: NICE NG101 (1.4.9) says to stage the axilla with sentinel lymph node biopsy rather than axillary lymph node clearance for people with invasive breast cancer who have no evidence of lymph node involvement on ultrasound or a negative ultrasound-guided needle biopsy, and (1.4.10) to perform it using the dual technique with isotope and blue dye. Macmillan says surgeons remove the smallest number of nodes possible, usually 1 to 3, which reduces the risk of arm swelling and shoulder stiffness.

What it saves. In the pooled prospective cohorts of the DiSipio meta-analysis, arm lymphoedema affected 5.6 percent of women after sentinel node biopsy against 19.9 percent after axillary lymph node dissection.

Where even a sentinel node biopsy may be avoidable. In INSEMA, 4,858 patients in the per-protocol analysis with clinically node-negative T1 or T2 cancer having breast-conserving surgery were randomised between omitting axillary surgery and sentinel node biopsy; 5-year invasive disease-free survival was 91.9 percent with omission and 91.7 percent with surgery (hazard ratio 0.91), and the omission group had less lymphoedema, greater arm mobility and less pain on moving the arm or shoulder. This is a trial result rather than a UK recommendation, and NG101 still asks for sentinel node biopsy.

records.name: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
records.tldr: Radiofrequency ablation passes alternating electrical current through tissue to generate heat near an electrode. The device reading does not establish complete tumour destruction.
records.summary:
In interstitial radiofrequency ablation, electrical resistance generates heat around an electrode and heat also spreads by conduction. Electrical and thermal tissue properties, exposure time, applicator placement and blood flow influence the injury zone. The whole target and intended margin must be assessed while protecting nearby structures.

The name does not specify a universal lesion size, a temperature everywhere in the tissue, equivalence to surgery or superiority over another ablation method. Procedural coverage, defined follow-up evidence of complete ablation, later local progression and complications are separate measurements.

notes: A perfused ex-vivo calf-liver experiment compared monopolar RF, bipolar RF and microwave devices. The ordering depended on the measured volume, mass, density and other outputs. Such device/model results do not establish a universal clinical winner.

records.name: Microwave ablation (MWA)
records.tldr: Microwave ablation uses an antenna and an oscillating electromagnetic field to heat tissue. Coverage depends on the device, tissue and exposure, rather than a universal advantage over other methods.
records.summary:
An antenna couples microwave energy into tissue. Polar molecules, especially water, respond to the oscillating electric field and tissue heats; heat also spreads by conduction. This differs from resistive heating by electrical current in radiofrequency ablation. Neither mechanism specifies the complete injury boundary.

A perfused ex-vivo calf-liver comparison found effects of flow on both RF and microwave measurements. The relative results depended on the device and measured output. Reduced effects in one setup do not mean immunity to heat loss or prove better local control in every clinical setting. Access, coverage, normal-tissue exposure, follow-up and complications remain separate questions.

records.name: Cryoablation
records.tldr: Cryoablation extracts heat through an applicator to freeze selected tissue. A visible ice ball does not show that every point received lethal exposure.
records.summary:
Freezing and thawing can injure cells through ice formation, osmotic changes and vascular injury. The historical mechanistic literature emphasises temperature, time, thawing and repetition; a probe setpoint is not exposure everywhere in the tissue. The visible frozen region and the lethal boundary need separate assessment.

Georgiades and colleagues studied normal renal tissue in swine. Measurements from six test animals found a mean nonlethal rim of 0.75 millimetres, with variation and widening near large vessels. Their proposed six-millimetre visible-ice margin for renal cancer was an extrapolation under stated assumptions, rather than a measured universal human margin.

Site, geometry, applicators and nearby structures affect feasibility and harm. Freezing, preserved material or local tissue destruction alone does not establish antigen presentation, useful immune priming or distant tumour control.

records.name: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT / SABR)
records.tldr: Stereotactic body radiotherapy delivers a high dose per treatment to a defined body target using specialised localisation and verification. A short schedule alone does not identify it or establish safety.
records.summary:
Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

records.name: IMRT / IGRT / VMAT (modern external beam radiotherapy)
records.tldr: Modern external beam techniques shape dose and use imaging to check position. They can reduce exposure to nearby healthy tissues, but do not eliminate it.
records.summary: Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) sculpts dose with a multileaf collimator; volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) does it while the machine rotates, in minutes; image guided radiotherapy (IGRT) uses repeated imaging to check treatment position and adjust treatment if needed. Shaping and verifying dose can limit normal tissue exposure but do not eliminate it. Together they cut xerostomia in head and neck cancer (PARSPORT), rectal toxicity in prostate cancer and allowed hypofractionation. Planning quality depends on contouring, now aided by AI auto-segmentation. Proton therapy adds a sharper depth stop for selected tumours.

records.name: Hypofractionation (fewer, larger radiotherapy doses)
records.tldr: Hypofractionation uses larger radiation doses per treatment than a specified comparison schedule, usually with fewer treatments. Control and harms depend on the whole tested regimen.
records.summary:
Hypofractionation uses larger doses per fraction relative to a stated conventional comparison, commonly with fewer treatments. Keep total gray, dose per fraction, count, spacing, overall duration and treatment volume together. For equal fractions, total physical dose is the fraction count multiplied by dose per fraction; this arithmetic does not establish biological equivalence. Acceleration changes overall timing; a boost changes the dose to a selected region. Hypofractionation does not by itself identify stereotactic delivery.

Biological response depends on tissue, repair and timing, rather than total physical dose alone. Alpha/beta is a model parameter in gray describing fraction-size sensitivity. Under the linear-quadratic model and its assumptions, a lower ratio predicts greater sensitivity to fraction size at the same total physical dose. Historical teaching values near 10 gray for early effects and 3 for late effects are conventions, not universal constants. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for tumour control, with confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, with interval 2.3 to 4.5. Keep the model, endpoint and uncertainty.

START-B compared 50 gray in 25 fractions over five weeks with 40 in 15 over three weeks after surgery for early breast cancer, assessing local-regional relapse and late effects. FAST-Forward tested 40 gray in 15 fractions over three weeks against 27 or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report supported non-inferiority of 26 gray for breast relapse under the trial margin; 27 gray produced more normal-tissue effects. These results do not validate every five-visit course, nodal field, reirradiation plan or immune-priming schedule.

notes: FAST-Forward randomised 4,096 people after surgery for early breast cancer to forty gray in fifteen fractions over three weeks, 27 in five over one week, or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report found 26 in five non-inferior for ipsilateral breast-tumour relapse under the prespecified margin; the five-year relapse estimate after forty gray was 2.1%. Normal-tissue assessments differed by regimen: 27 produced more effects, whereas 26 did not show that increase versus forty. These are local-control and normal-tissue results in the tested setting, not a demonstration that a five-visit course is SBRT or an immune optimum.

records.name: Gray unit (Gy)
records.tldr: Gray measures absorbed radiation energy per mass: one joule per kilogram. It is not the percentage of cells killed and does not by itself specify biological effect.
records.summary:
Gray is a unit of absorbed radiation dose: one joule of energy deposited per kilogram of material. It does not state what fraction of cells died. The same absorbed dose can have different biological effects in different tissues or when delivered with different timing and fractionation. Total dose alone does not establish equivalent schedules.

Activity describes nuclear transformations per second and is measured in becquerels. Absorbed dose describes deposited energy per mass and is measured in gray. An administered activity and the absorbed dose in a particular tissue are different quantities.
